newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end sharply lower, led by gold.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end sharply lower, led by gold.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended sharply lower Friday, led by gold which fell to new three year lows, as commodity funds increased their short positions, in a market still lacking players due to the New Year holidays.

"The rise of US bond yields in recent days, reducing the attractiveness of holding physical assets, and the surge in the dollar, weakening demand for gold in other currencies, has weighed on precious metals prices this week," Refco New York analyst Tim Porter said.

COMEX February gold tumbled $4.60 to close at $362.00 an ounce, after posting a new life-of-contract low at $361.80, with contract lows seen in all deliveries out to December 1997. Total estimated gold futures volume was 60,000 lots.
Spot gold in the bullion market ended quoted $360.75/361.25, after fixing at a new three year low at $364.00 in London Friday afternoon, compared to the New York close Thursday at $365.25/75.
"With the US stock market still strong, there's just no investment demand for gold, leaving commodity funds to push gold lower," CPM Group analyst Edward Kempf said.

Short term implied lease rates jumped again this week, suggesting renewed short selling in the bullion market, while New Year holidays kept potential trade buyers and small investors in Asia out of the market, traders said.
COMEX gold futures open interest rose rose a further 4,711 lots to 194,516 lots Thursday, suggesting commodity funds were adding to their already large net short positions.

February gold again looks oversold though, with a standard nine-day relative strength indicator (RSI) for February gold closing at 12.57 percent Friday, suggesting a further period of consolidation could ensue, analysts said.
But after breaking down out of its $366-370 range of the past month, longer term spot gold could fall to $360 or even $340, levels last seen in 1993, analysts said.

Physical demand remains soft with CRU International reporting shipments of gold bullion into the big six entrepot import markets (Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Dubai and Turkey) down 13 percent in the first 10 months of 1996.

Meanwhile, uncertainty about the role of gold in the new single European currency system due in 1999, and the potential for further European central bank gold sales in 1997, continues to afford the bears some protection, analysts said.

European central banks hold about 460 million ounces of gold, over 40 percent of all official holdings worldwide, but have not decided what to do with their reserves when they surrender their monetary policy powers to the planned European central bank.
Silver held up relatively well Friday though, with the spot gold/silver ratio slipping to 77.24 at the close from 77.53 at Thursday's close.

COMEX March silver ended down 4.7 cents at $4.685 an ounce, after posting a new contract low at $4.670, with new contract lows seen in all deliveries out to December 1997 also. Total estimated silver futures volume was 22,000 lots.

COMEX silver futures open interest rose 1,269 lots to 85,962 lots Thursday, but open interest fell 1,229 lots to 57,589 in the active March contract, suggesting funds were reducing their recent small net long positions, analysts said.
Silver fixed at $4.703 in London Friday morning, its lowest fix since March 1995.
COMEX silver stocks, which include Wilmington Trust depositary stocks from January 2, rose 600,338 ounces Thursday to 204,051,121 ounces.
NYMEX April platinum closed down $3.20 at $367.90 an ounce, after seeing a fresh life-of-contract low at $367.50, with all deliveries out to January 1998 seeing contract lows also.
Platinum fixed at $366.50 an ounce in London Friday morning, the lowest fix since November 2, 1993.
The April gold/platinum spread recovered to $4.30 an ounce by the close, from $2.40 an ounce Thursday.
NYMEX March palladium ended down $1.50 at $121.75, correcting from its run up Tuesday, after palladium fixed at a 15 week high at $120.75 in London Thursday.
